He was proficient in calculating odds, and could pilot speeders. ==Behind the scenes== [[File:MCQ-counterparts.jpg|thumb|left|210px|Concept art of C-3PO and R2-D2 by Ralph McQuarrie]] ===Origins=== {{Quote|I'm See Threepio, Human-Cyborg Relations. Your kindness is greatly appreciated.|See Threepio on several occasions in the rough draft of ''The Star Wars''|{{WebCite|url=http://www.starwarz.com/starkiller/scripts/thestarwars_rough_draft.htm|text=THE STAR WARS by George Lucas - Rough Draft|work=Starkiller - The Jedi Bendu Script Site|archivedate=20100524014638}}}} Although C-3PO and R2-D2 did not appear in [[1973]]'s original fourteen-page [[The Star Wars story synopsis|story synopsis of "The Star Wars,"]]{{WebCite|url=http://www.starwarz.com/starkiller/scripts/thestarwars_synopsis.htm|text=THE STAR WARS Story Synopsis|archivedate=20100113004912}} their characters were featured in the 132-page [[The Star Wars rough draft|rough draft]] of "The [[Star Wars]]," completed in [[May]] [[1974]], as See Threepio and Artoo Detoo. Threepio is described as being tall, thin, old, battered, and of Human proportions, and the two droids are written as construction robots in an Imperial Space Fortress. As the Fortress is attacked by [[Aquillian Ranger/Legends|Aquilaean]] starships, Threepio is the robot who decides to abandon ship, while ARTWO is hesitant to desert their duty. The two then land in the dune sea of [[Utapau/Legends|Utapau]], where they meet [[Annikin Starkiller|Starkiller]]. By [[1975]], when [[George Lucas]] had written ''[[Adventures of the Starkiller, Episode I: The Star Wars]]'', the story began with the two droids aboard a Rebel spacefighter and oriented itself around their evacuation, landing on Utapau, and being captured by Jawas.{{WebCite|url=http://www.starwarz.com/starkiller/scripts/thestarwars_second_draft.htm|text=ADVENTURES OF THE STARKILLER (episode one) - "The Star Wars" by George Lucas|archivedate=20020809190949}} With relatively few changes, this storyline went on to appear in the original [[Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope|''Star Wars'' film]]. When creating the characters of C-3PO and R2-D2, Lucas looked to [[Wikipedia:Akira Kurosawa|Akira Kurosawa's]] 1958 film [[Wikipedia:The Hidden Fortress|''The Hidden Fortress'']], which he credits as one of his inspirations for ''Star Wars''. ''The Hidden Fortress'' is told from the point of view of the peasantsThe Characters of ''Star Wars'' - [[Star Wars Trilogy (DVD)]] Tahei and Matashichi,{{WebCite|url=http://bushidodreams.com/2009/07/the-genius-of-kurosawa-the-hidden-fortress|text=The Genius of Kurosawa – The Hidden Fortress|nobackup=1}} who are the film's comic relief duo that travel Japan in the company of a General and a Princess, and, despite coming from the lowest possible social class, are privy to an adventure taking place on a grand level of international diplomacy. Lucas thus wrote C-3PO and R2-D2 into ''Star Wars'' as similar comic characters and narrators to ''The Hidden Fortress''{{'s}} peasants. Lucas felt that the two droids had to be very different from one another in both personality and appearance, and envisioned an elegant and sophisticated anthropomorphic design for C-3PO, whom he saw as coming from an elegant and sophisticated environment. C-3PO's original appearance, visible in concept art by [[Ralph McQuarrie]], was based on The Maschinenmensch, the robot from the 1927 silent film [[Wikipedia:Metropolis (film)|''Metropolis'']]. Lucas wanted C-3PO's face to be a completely neutral one that the viewer could read emotion into based on the droid's environment, and conceived of the character's personality as being akin to a used-car salesman who would say whatever was necessary to please others. In an early draft for ''The Phantom Menace'', C-3PO's original name was CPO. The 3 was then added when Padmé told Anakin Skywalker that her favorite number was 3.{{WebCite|url=http://theforce.net/episode1/cutting_room/cutting_room_03.asp|text=TheForce.Net - Episode I - Cutting Room Floor - Page 3|archivedate=20190730110754}} ===Portrayal=== {{Quote|I didn't want to go, because [my agent] said it's the part of a robot, so I said 'You're mad! I don't play robots.' |Anthony Daniels, on his audition for the part of C-3PO|{{WordPress|subdomain=dailypop|url=2007/06/01|name=The Daily Pop|text=Anthony Daniels interview|date=2007-06-01|archivedate=20160917231337}}}} [[File:Anthonydaniels.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Anthony Daniels, the man behind C-3PO]] British actor [[Anthony Daniels]] was cast in the role of C-3PO, having both the slender build necessary to fit into the costume, and training as a [[Wikipedia:mime artist|mime artist]].''[[Empire of Dreams: The Story of the Star Wars Trilogy]]'' Daniels was hesitant to audition for the part of a robot, but after being convinced by his agent to meet George Lucas and read ''Star Wars''{{'s}} script, he began to feel that C-3PO was a very likable character with a large personality. McQuarrie's painting of C-3PO and R2-D2 also played a role in convincing Daniels to take the part, as he saw a vulnerability in the character's face that invoked pity. Rather than play C-3PO as a used-car salesman, Daniels channeled the voice of a fussy British butler, feeling that it fit the character's personality. Lucas briefly considered casting another actor to provide the droid's voice, but was convinced by sound designer [[Ben Burtt]], among others, that Daniels's vocal performance was an excellent one that he had synchronized well with his body motions. Daniels thus re-recorded every line of C-3PO's dialogue.{{WebCite|url=http://www.anthonydaniels.com/biography/content.html|text=Biography|archivedate=20200731020414}} Burtt credits Daniels's complete performance as having created a total character. Following the success of ''Star Wars'' in [[1977]],{{WebCite|url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/title/tt0076759|text=Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope (1977)|archivedate=20191222175710}} Daniels reprised his role as C-3PO in the film's two sequels, [[1980]]'s [[Star Wars: Episode V The Empire Strikes Back|''The Empire Strikes Back'']] and [[1983]]'s [[Star Wars: Episode VI Return of the Jedi|''Return of the Jedi'']]. He reprised the role again in all three ''Star Wars'' [[Prequel trilogy|prequels]], respectively released in [[1999]], [[2002]], and [[2005]]. Daniels is the only actor to appear in all six of Legends' primary ''Star Wars'' films, and was also in ''[[Star Wars: Clone Wars]]'', ''[[Star Wars: The Clone Wars]]'', ''[[Star Wars: Droids: The Adventures of R2-D2 and C-3PO]]'', and ''[[The Star Wars Holiday Special]]''. Daniels also voiced C-3PO in all three radio dramas of the original ''Star Wars'' trilogy[[Star Wars (radio)|''Star Wars'' radio drama]][[Return of the Jedi (radio)|''Return of the Jedi'' radio drama]] (for which he made notations in the scripts and revised C-3PO's dialogue),Forward to [[Star Wars Omnibus: Droids|''Omnibus: Droids'']] and in the [[Star Wars video games|video game]] ''[[Star Wars: Pit Droids]]''.''[[Star Wars: Pit Droids]]'' Outside the ''Star Wars'' [[Canon|continuity]], Daniels has guest-starred as C-3PO in a number of appearances, including guest roles on ''[[The Muppet Show]]'', ''[[Sesame Street]]'', [[Wikipedia:Jeopardy!|''Jeopardy!'']], [[Wikipedia:Donny & Marie (1976 TV series)|''The Donny and Marie Show'']], and at the [[Wikipedia:Academy Award|Academy Awards]]. He has also played the droid in [[Infinities|non-canon]] ''Star Wars'' material such as 1977's ''[[The Making of Star Wars]]'' television special, 1980's [[Christmas in the Stars|''Christmas in the Stars: Star Wars Christmas Album'']].''[[Christmas in the Stars]]'' Daniels's C-3PO résumé further includes public service announcements concerned with whooping cough immunizations{{WebCite|url=http://technabob.com/blog/2009/10/24/r2-d2-c-3po-revealed|text=Behind the Scenes of a Star Wars Psa Reveals C-3PO & R2-D2′S Secret|author=Varias, Lambert|date=2009-10-24|archivedate=20161010082800}} and [[Star Wars Anti-Smoking PSA|anti-smoking campaigns]], as well as commercials for C-3PO-themed breakfast cereal and children's underwear.{{WebCite|url=http://blog.sfgate.com/parenting/2009/10/06/c-3po-still-wants-you-to-stop-smoking|text=C-3PO still wants you to stop smoking …|author=Hartlaub, Peter|date=2009-10-06|archivedate=20171122133032}} [[Jim Ward (voice actor)|Jim Ward]] provided the voice of C-3PO and a few other characters in the three ''[[Star Wars: Dark Empire]]'' audio dramas.[[Dark Empire (audio drama)|''Dark Empire'' audio drama]][[Dark Empire II (audio drama)|''Dark Empire II'' audio drama]][[Empire's End (audio drama)|''Empire's End'' audio drama]] During filming of ''The Phantom Menace'', [[Industrial Light & Magic]] Chief Model maker [[Michael Lynch]] built a puppet that was used to portray C-3PO's unfinished appearance, with Daniels providing the character's voice. C-3PO's motions were realized by Lynch acting as a puppeteer dressed in a full-color suit, at times on-set with the other actors and at others filmed against a green screen. Daniels remained off-camera and delivered the lines, guiding Lynch's movements as he brought the puppet to life.{{SWArchive|url=episode-i/bts/production/f19991102/index.html|text=The Man (Literally) Behind C-3PO}} ====Costume==== {{Quote|If you've ever met [producer] Rick McCallum, you'll know they're not about to make a new costume every time we do this thing, so I'm actually wearing the same costume as I did back then.|Anthony Daniels in 2005|{{WebCite|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/films/2005/05/18/anthony_daniels_star_wars_episode_iii_interview.shtml|text=Movies - interview - Anthony Daniels|author=Brett, Anwar|archivedate=20161017014758}}}} [[File:AnthonyDanielsisastandupguy.jpg|thumb|left|205px|Unable to sit down, Anthony Daniels had to lean against a board while wearing his C-3PO costume during the shooting of ''Star Wars''.]] The C-3PO costume was constructed such that Daniels could not sit down while wearing it; he thus had to lean against a board to rest between shots. Scenes where C-3PO sits down required the costume to be partially disassembled.''[[The Making of Star Wars: The Definitive Story Behind the Original Film]]''{{WebCite|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2006/07/05/star-wars-secrets-off-camera-action|text=Star Wars Secrets: Off-Camera Action|author=Gilchrist, Todd|date=2006-07-05|archivedate=20160513125138}} The costume was in part created by Liz Moore, who had previously designed the star child in [[Wikipedia:2001: A Space Odyssey (film)|''2001: A Space Odyssey'']], a film that Daniels had walked out of, but later appreciated.{{WebCite|url=http://seattletimes.nwsource.com/html/thearts/2010034957_starwars12.html|text=A Q&A with Anthony Daniels (C3PO), touring with "Star Wars: In Concert"|author=Keogh, Tom|date=2009-10-12|archivedate=20091016070250}} Filming for ''Star Wars'' began in [[Tunisia]], and on the first day of shooting, the costume was yet to be completed. The combined efforts of six people were able to dress Daniels completely in a total of two hours.{{WebCite|url=http://www.etc.cmu.edu/global_news/?q=node/229|text=Anthony Daniels interview in December issue of Pittsburgh Magazine|author=Melada, Geoffrey W.|date=2008-12-17|archivedate=20110623222836}} Twenty-five years later, Daniels wore the same costume while working on the prequel trilogy. In [[2009]] and [[2010]], the C-3PO costume toured with ''[[Star Wars: In Concert]]'', being displayed in the exhibition area of each arena.{{WebCite|url=http://blogs.riverfronttimes.com/atoz/2009/12/a_polite_chat_with_anthony_daniels_voice_of_c3po_star_wars_in_concert_tour_holiday_special_st_louis_meco_symphony_john_williams_movie_scores.php|text=A Polite Chat with Anthony Daniels, the Voice of ''Star Wars''{{'}} C-3PO, who Comes to St. Louis Thursday for ''Star Wars In Concert''|author=Nick Lucchesi|date=2009-12-09|archivedate=20100420041646}} ===In ''Star Wars'' media=== {{Quote|Some of the pages are as convincing in character to me, as though I were actually there, playing the part. When a character you have created and loved has been reproduced commercially in every way from bubble bath to bubble gum, you can get a little protective. But with these stories, I know Threepio is safe.|Anthony Daniels on Dark Horse Comics' ''Droids'' series|}} In addition to appearing in all six principal episodes of ''Star Wars'', C-3PO holds the honor of speaking the first and last lines of the entire saga. In the opening scene of the original ''Star Wars'', the protocol droid kicks off the film's dialogue by asking R2-D2, "Did you hear that? They've shut down the main reactor. We'll be destroyed for sure! This is madness." Nearly thirty years later, the spoken portions of ''Revenge of the Sith'' concluded with C-3PO reacting to the news that he would receive a memory wipe by uttering "Oh no!" The respective scenes both take place aboard the starship ''Tantive IV'', and were filmed on the same set. Outside of Episodes I through VI, C-3PO has appeared in myriad works within the [[Star Wars Legends|Expanded Universe]]. Along with his counterpart, R2-D2, he starred in an animated series on [[ABC Television Network|ABC]], as well as [[Star Wars comic books|comic books]] based on the series published by [[Marvel Comics|Marvel]] and [[Dark Horse Comics]].[[Star Wars: Droids (1986)|''Star Wars: Droids'' (1986)]][[Star Wars: Droids (1994)|''Star Wars: Droids'' (1994)]] C-3PO and R2-D2 played prominent roles in many of the novels published by [[Bantam Spectra]] throughout the 1990s taking place in the years following ''Return of the Jedi'', sometimes accompanying Luke, Han, and Leia, and sometimes being caught up in adventures of their own. When [[Del Rey]] took over ''Star Wars'' novel publishing in 1999, the droid duo faded into the background somewhat as a new generation of heroes developed,''[[Star Wars: The New Jedi Order]]'' although C-3PO did undergo a character arc that involved him contemplating the prospect of deactivation and questioning his own mortality.''[[The New Jedi Order: Agents of Chaos I: Hero's Trial]]'' [[In-universe]], C-3PO is still faithfully serving the Skywalker and Solo families forty-three years after the events of the original ''Star Wars''. His origins were laid down by George Lucas via a tape recorder in 1977, who established that he had been constructed on the world of Affa and later reassembled by a young boy working for a junk dealer. Lucas reused the latter half of this concept in ''The Phantom Menace'', and the former half was canonized by the [[StarWars.com]] [[Databank (original)|Databank]]. ====Continuity peculiarities==== C-3PO's name is often erroneously spelled C-3P0, even in official sources. In the novel ''[[Legacy of the Force: Tempest]]'', he is described as dropping his chin, despite not having one.''[[Legacy of the Force: Tempest]]'' In [[Star Wars: A New Hope (novelization)|the novelization of ''A New Hope'']], C-3PO once refers to himself as "CV-3PO" when introducing himself to Owen Lars. In this passage, C-3PO claims that "V" stands for his "middle name," "Versatility." [[Leland Chee]] has indicated that this is not to be taken literally as part of the droid's official name.{{Twitter|HolocronKeeper|status/386601312332173312|[[Leland Chee]]|quote=@reeldefiction Are there really people out there thinking that "Versatility" is part of 3PO's official designation?|archivedate=20190722103238}} ===Actor and author comments=== {{Quote|As I look up through the clouds and to the sun, I'm wondering where did [C-3PO] come from? But I'm very glad he certainly did end up in my pocket.|Anthony Daniels|}} In a 2009 interview, he stated that the character has never left him, and expressed his fondness for the droid. Although he has at times considered moving on to other things, the notion has never remained with him for very long. He feels that he knows the character better than anyone, and sees C-3PO as being like his best friend,{{SWArchive|url=theclonewars/news20090127.html|text=C-3PO Plays a Pivotal Role in "Trespass"}} one that he feels a responsibility to continue playing, else C-3PO would be very upset.{{WebCite|url=http://www.bigshinyrobot.com/reviews/archives/7319|text=COMIC-CON INTERVIEW: Anthony Daniels talks Star Wars|author=Swank-mo-tron|date=2009-08-08|archivedate=20110827011347}} He also admits to feeling protective of the character. Daniels maintains that he himself is very different from C-3PO, and has called the character a "strange creation that came out of somewhere," but nevertheless a creation that he is proud of. [[File:Kersh07_bg.jpg|thumb|right|225px|Anthony Daniels rehearses a scene with director [[Irvin Kershner]] during filming of ''The Empire Strikes Back''.]] From his first read-throughs of the script of ''Star Wars'', Daniels thought that C-3PO had a likable personality; he sees the character as not heroic, but very thoughtful, loyal, and loving, traits that make up for his uptightness and complete lack of a sense of humor or irony. He has described the droid as being loyal to his final nut and bolt, and therefore someone who would remain at a friend's side until the end of the droid's existence. Daniels cites portraying C-3PO as having been a considerable challenge. As [[Kenny Baker]], playing R2-D2, could not talk to him during shooting, perfecting their comic timing proved difficult. Speaking in C-3PO's voice is also challenging, as it creates tension and uptightness in his back muscles, leaving them knotted and sore after a recording session. As C-3PO is not a relaxed character, Daniels cannot perform the voice in a relaxed manner. He also cites difficulties involved with wearing the suit as obstacles that he had to overcome while shooting the [[original trilogy]]. Daniels's voice work has been praised by [[Dave Filoni]], the supervising director of the animated series ''Star Wars: The Clone Wars'', who credits Daniels as having fantastic insight into every word and phrase spoken by C-3PO, and as able to adapt nearly every line to the character's cadence. While seeking writers for Dark Horse Comics' ''Droids'' series, editors [[Ryder Windham]] and [[Dan Thorsland]] were dismayed that many of their potential hirees regarded C-3PO and R2-D2 as little more than comic relief. The two eventually settled on Thorsland himself to write the series, who felt that the droid duo were intelligent machines that often found themselves in an unfortunate plight, being treated worse than slaves. Daniels later praised Thorsland's writing of C-3PO and wrote an introduction for [[Star Wars: Droids: The Kalarba Adventures|one]] of the series' [[Star Wars comic books|trade paperbacks]]. When writing [[2003]]'s ''[[The New Jedi Order: The Unifying Force]]'', the finale of the nineteen-book series [[Star Wars: The New Jedi Order|''The New Jedi Order'']], author [[James Luceno]] found himself drawn to C-3PO, among other characters, as the droid had been forced to rethink many truths he had long accepted throughout the series.{{WebCite|url=http://www.theforce.net/books/unjoh/interviews/lucenotos.html|text=Wrapping It All Up - An Interview with James Luceno|work=The Unofficial NJO Homepage|archivedate=20200201043532}} ===Impact on popular culture=== {{Quote|After all, Threepio is as much an icon of Star Wars as Darth Vader.|Dave Filoni|}} [[File:Cereal_Box_C3P0s.jpg|thumb|left|120px|A crunchy new Force at breakfast]] As a principal character in a wildly popular film saga, C-3PO has become a cultural icon of sorts, having been referred to as one of the most iconic characters in all of popular science fiction.{{WebCite|url=http://www.houstonpress.com/music/talking-with-c-3po-himself-anthony-daniels-about-star-wars-in-concert-6501753|text=Talking With C-3PO Himself, Anthony Daniels, About Star Wars: In Concert|author=Hlavaty, Craig|date=2009-10-22|work=Rocks Off|archivedate=20150910031201}} A wide variety of C-3PO merchandise has been produced over the years, including scores of action figures,{{KennerCite|set=Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (toy line)|pack=See-Threepio (C-3PO) With Removable Limbs|link=VINtC3POlimbs.asp}}{{KennerCite|set=Star Wars: The Power of the Force (1995 toy line)|pack=C-3PO with Realistic Metalized Body|link=POTF2c3po.asp}}{{HasbroCite|set=Star Wars: Episode I (toy line)|pack=C-3PO|altlink=http://www.rebelscum.com/episodeIC3PO.asp}}{{HasbroCite|set=Star Wars: The Original Trilogy Collection|pack=C-3PO|altlink=https://www.rebelscum.com/OTC13c3po.asp}}{{HasbroCite|set=Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith (toy line)|pack=#18: C-3PO|altlink=https://www.rebelscum.com/ROTS0518c-3po.asp}} busts,{{GentleGiantCite|set=Collectible Mini Bust|pack=C-3PO|altlink=https://www.rebelscum.com/gg04c3po.asp}} a life-sized figure,{{SideshowCite|set=Life-size Figure|pack=C-3PO|altlink=http://www.mwctoys.com/REVIEW_022509b.htm}} pez dispensers,{{WebCite|url=http://www.pezdispenser.org/star-wars-pez-dispensers/12-tall-c3po-star-wars-pez-dispenser-2|text=12″ Tall C3po Star Wars Pez Dispenser|nobackup=1}} and even a breakfast cereal.
